title: Aggregation & Grouping
tagline: COUNT, SUM, AVG — the grammar of summarizing

placementQuiz.explain: COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values in that column.
Aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, etc.) ignore NULL values automatically.

placementQuiz.q: GROUP BY dept_id — one row per:
placementQuiz.explain: GROUP BY collapses rows with same dept_id into one group. One output row per department.

options: WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups
HAVING filters rows; WHERE filters groups
placementQuiz.explain: WHERE runs before GROUP BY (row filter). HAVING runs after GROUP BY (group filter).

placementQuiz.q: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees; without GROUP BY:
options: One row: total count, dept_id = NULL
placementQuiz.explain: Mixing aggregate (COUNT) with non-aggregated column (dept_id) without GROUP BY is invalid SQL.

blocks.md: GROUP BY is a funnel: many rows enter, they're sorted by key, identical keys merge into one row. Aggregates (COUNT, SUM, AVG) compute on each bucket.

items: Every non-aggregate column in SELECT must be in GROUP BY
NULLs group together (all NULLs = one group)
Aggregate functions: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, STRING_AGG
ORDER BY runs after GROUP BY — can use aliases

items.q: COUNT(*) vs COUNT(manager_id) when 10 employees, 3 have NULL manager:
items.explain: COUNT(*) = all rows (10). COUNT(manager_id) = non-NULL only (7).

sections.title: Core Aggregates — COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX

blocks.label: basic aggregates
blocks.code:
-- COUNT: row count (includes NULL rows)
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees;
-- COUNT(col): non-NULL count
SELECT COUNT(manager_id) FROM employees;

-- SUM, AVG: numeric only
SELECT SUM(salary), AVG(salary) FROM employees;

-- MIN, MAX: any comparable type
SELECT MIN(hire_date), MAX(hire_date) FROM employees;

-- Multiple aggregates at once
SELECT dept_id,
  COUNT(*) AS emp_count,
  SUM(salary) AS total_pay,
  AVG(salary) AS avg_pay,
  MIN(salary) AS min_pay,
  MAX(salary) AS max_pay
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id;
blocks.pg:
-- STRING_AGG for concatenation
SELECT dept_id, STRING_AGG(name, ', ') FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id;
blocks.mysql:
-- GROUP_CONCAT for concatenation
SELECT dept_id, GROUP_CONCAT(name SEPARATOR ', ') FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id;
blocks.py-pandas:
# Aggregation
grouped = employees.groupby('dept_id').agg(
    emp_count=('id', 'count'),
    total_pay=('salary', 'sum'),
    avg_pay=('salary', 'mean'),
    min_pay=('salary', 'min'),
    max_pay=('salary', 'max')
).reset_index()

items.q: GROUP BY dept_id, status with 5 depts and 3 statuses — max groups:
items.explain: Max groups = 5 depts × 3 statuses = 15. Actual may be fewer if some combos missing.

items.q: GROUP BY EXTRACT(MONTH FROM hire_date) — groups by:
items.explain: EXTRACT(MONTH FROM date) returns 1-12. Groups by month across all years.

blocks.label: group by multiple
blocks.code:
-- Group by dept AND status
SELECT dept_id, status, COUNT(*)
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id, status;
-- One row per (dept_id, status) combination

-- Group by expression
SELECT EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date) AS yr, COUNT(*)
FROM employees
GROUP BY EXTRACT(YEAR FROM hire_date);
blocks.pg:
-- GROUP BY can use expressions
SELECT date_trunc('month', created_at) AS month, COUNT(*)
FROM events
GROUP BY date_trunc('month', created_at);
blocks.mysql: SELECT YEAR(hire_date) AS yr, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY YEAR(hire_date);
blocks.py-pandas:
# Multi-column groupby
grouped = employees.groupby(['dept_id', 'status']).size().reset_index(name='count')

# Expression groupby
grouped = employees.groupby(employees['hire_date'].dt.year).size()

blocks.label: having clause
blocks.code:
-- Departments with > 10 employees
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 10;

-- HAVING can use aliases (PostgreSQL)
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING cnt > 10;

-- Multiple HAVING conditions
SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000 AND COUNT(*) > 5;
blocks.pg:
-- Can use column alias in HAVING
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id HAVING cnt > 10;
blocks.mysql:
-- MySQL: alias in HAVING works
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id HAVING cnt > 10;
blocks.py-pandas:
# Having = filter after groupby
grouped = employees.groupby('dept_id').size().reset_index(name='cnt')
result = grouped[grouped['cnt'] > 10]

items.explain: WHERE = row filter (pre-GROUP BY). HAVING = group filter (post-GROUP BY).

items.q: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees HAVING COUNT(*) > 5; without GROUP BY:
items.explain: No GROUP BY → single group (whole table). HAVING filters that one group.

blocks.text: Problem: Total payroll, average salary, and headcount per department

items.title: Employee Count per Department
items.statement: Count employees in each department. Return dept_id and emp_count.

approaches.name: Brute
approaches.idea: Correlated subquery per department: run a separate COUNT for each dept_id.

code.code:
SELECT d.dept_id,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id) AS emp_count
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT dept_id FROM employees) d
ORDER BY d.dept_id;
code.mysql:
SELECT d.dept_id,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id) AS emp_count
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT dept_id FROM employees) d
ORDER BY d.dept_id;
code.py-pandas:
result = []
for dept in employees['dept_id'].drop_duplicates():
    cnt = len(employees[employees['dept_id'] == dept])
    result.append({'dept_id': dept, 'emp_count': cnt})
pd.DataFrame(result)

approaches.cost: O(departments × employees) — re-scans employees for each department. Fine for 7 depts, not for 10k.
approaches.pitfalls: Drive the loop from the dept_ids that appear in employees. Driving it from departments adds the empty Research dept (7 rows, not 6): that answers a different question, the LEFT JOIN variant.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Single scan with GROUP BY — hash or sort aggregation in one pass.

code.code:
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS emp_count
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
ORDER BY dept_id;
code.mysql: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS emp_count FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id ORDER BY dept_id;

approaches.cost: One full scan of employees (21 rows) + hash aggregate. O(n) time, O(groups) memory.

exercise.solution: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS emp_count FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id ORDER BY dept_id;

items.title: Average Salary per Department
items.statement: Average salary for each department. Return dept_id and avg_salary rounded to 2 decimals.

approaches.name: Brute
approaches.idea: Correlated subquery computing AVG per department — re-scans employees for each dept.

code.code:
SELECT d.dept_id,
  ROUND((SELECT AVG(salary)::numeric FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id AND e.salary IS NOT NULL), 2) AS avg_salary
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT dept_id FROM employees) d
ORDER BY d.dept_id;
code.mysql:
SELECT d.dept_id,
  ROUND((SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id AND e.salary IS NOT NULL), 2) AS avg_salary
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT dept_id FROM employees) d
ORDER BY d.dept_id;
code.py-pandas:
result = []
for dept in employees['dept_id'].drop_duplicates():
    subset = employees[(employees['dept_id'] == dept) & (employees['salary'].notna())]
    avg_sal = round(subset['salary'].mean(), 2) if len(subset) > 0 else None
    result.append({'dept_id': dept, 'avg_salary': avg_sal})
pd.DataFrame(result)

approaches.cost: O(departments × employees) — re-scans for each department. AVG ignores NULLs automatically.
approaches.pitfalls: Drive the loop from the dept_ids that appear in employees. Driving it from departments adds the empty Research dept (7 rows, not 6): that answers a different question, the LEFT JOIN variant.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Single GROUP BY pass with AVG — one scan, hash aggregate, NULLs ignored automatically.

code.code:
SELECT dept_id, ROUND(AVG(salary)::numeric, 2) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY dept_id
ORDER BY dept_id;
code.mysql: SELECT dept_id, ROUND(AVG(salary), 2) AS avg_salary FROM employees WHERE salary IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id ORDER BY dept_id;

approaches.cost: One scan of employees (21 rows) + hash aggregate. O(n) time. WHERE filters NULLs before grouping.

exercise.solution: SELECT dept_id, ROUND(AVG(salary)::numeric, 2) AS avg_salary FROM employees WHERE salary IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id ORDER BY dept_id;

items.title: Total Payroll per Department
items.statement: Sum of salaries per department. Return dept_id and total_payroll.
hints: NULL salaries are ignored by SUM

approaches.name: Brute
approaches.idea: Correlated subquery per department — sums salaries for each dept separately.

code.code:
SELECT d.dept_id,
  (SELECT SUM(salary) FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id) AS total_payroll
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT dept_id FROM employees) d
ORDER BY d.dept_id;
code.mysql:
SELECT d.dept_id,
  (SELECT SUM(salary) FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id) AS total_payroll
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT dept_id FROM employees) d
ORDER BY d.dept_id;
code.py-pandas:
result = []
for dept in employees['dept_id'].drop_duplicates():
    total = employees[employees['dept_id'] == dept]['salary'].sum()
    result.append({'dept_id': dept, 'total_payroll': float(total) if not pd.isna(total) else 0})
pd.DataFrame(result)

approaches.cost: O(departments × employees) — re-scans employees for each department. SUM ignores NULLs; COALESCE handles empty groups.
approaches.pitfalls: Drive the loop from the dept_ids that appear in employees. Driving it from departments adds the empty Research dept (7 rows, not 6): that answers a different question, the LEFT JOIN variant.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Single GROUP BY with SUM — one pass, hash aggregate. SUM ignores NULLs automatically.

code.code:
SELECT dept_id, SUM(salary) AS total_payroll
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
ORDER BY dept_id;
code.mysql: SELECT dept_id, SUM(salary) AS total_payroll FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id ORDER BY dept_id;

approaches.cost: One scan of employees + hash aggregate. O(n) time. Departments with no employees don't appear (use LEFT JOIN from departments if needed).

exercise.solution: SELECT dept_id, SUM(salary) AS total_payroll FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id ORDER BY dept_id;

items.title: Min/Max Salary per Department
items.statement: Minimum and maximum salary in each department. Return dept_id, min_salary, max_salary.

approaches.name: Brute
approaches.idea: Two correlated subqueries per department — one for MIN, one for MAX.

code.code:
SELECT d.dept_id,
  (SELECT MIN(salary) FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id) AS min_salary,
  (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id) AS max_salary
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT dept_id FROM employees) d
ORDER BY d.dept_id;
code.mysql:
SELECT d.dept_id,
  (SELECT MIN(salary) FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id) AS min_salary,
  (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id) AS max_salary
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT dept_id FROM employees) d
ORDER BY d.dept_id;
code.py-pandas:
result = []
for dept in employees['dept_id'].drop_duplicates():
    subset = employees[employees['dept_id'] == dept]['salary'].dropna()
    mn = subset.min() if len(subset) > 0 else None
    mx = subset.max() if len(subset) > 0 else None
    result.append({'dept_id': dept, 'min_salary': mn, 'max_salary': mx})
pd.DataFrame(result)

approaches.cost: O(departments × employees) — two full scans per department. MIN/MAX ignore NULLs.
approaches.pitfalls: Drive the loop from the dept_ids that appear in employees. Driving it from departments adds the empty Research dept (7 rows, not 6): that answers a different question, the LEFT JOIN variant.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Single GROUP BY with MIN and MAX — one scan computes both aggregates simultaneously.

code.code:
SELECT dept_id, MIN(salary) AS min_salary, MAX(salary) AS max_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
ORDER BY dept_id;
code.mysql: SELECT dept_id, MIN(salary) AS min_salary, MAX(salary) AS max_salary FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id ORDER BY dept_id;

approaches.cost: One scan + hash aggregate. MIN/MAX computed together. O(n) time, O(groups) memory.

exercise.solution: SELECT dept_id, MIN(salary) AS min_salary, MAX(salary) AS max_salary FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id ORDER BY dept_id;

items.title: Departments with More Than 5 Employees
items.statement: Departments having more than 5 employees. Return dept_id and emp_count.

approaches.name: Brute
approaches.idea: Correlated subquery with HAVING simulated in WHERE — count per dept, then filter.

code.code:
SELECT d.dept_id, cnt AS emp_count
FROM departments d
JOIN (
  SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt
  FROM employees
  GROUP BY dept_id
) e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id
WHERE e.cnt > 5
ORDER BY d.dept_id;
code.mysql:
SELECT d.dept_id, e.cnt AS emp_count
FROM departments d
JOIN (
  SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id
) e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id
WHERE e.cnt > 5
ORDER BY d.dept_id;

approaches.cost: Two steps: GROUP BY (hash aggregate) then filter. Still scans employees once. Subquery materialization overhead.
approaches.pitfalls: Derived table forces materialization. HAVING pushes filter into aggregate — more efficient.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: HAVING clause — filter groups during aggregation, no derived table needed.

code.code:
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS emp_count
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
ORDER BY dept_id;
code.mysql: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS emp_count FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 ORDER BY dept_id;

approaches.cost: Single scan + hash aggregate with early filter. HAVING evaluated during grouping — optimal.

exercise.solution: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS emp_count FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 ORDER BY dept_id;

items.title: Employee Count by Dept and Job Title
items.statement: Count employees grouped by department AND job title. Return dept_id, job_title, emp_count.

approaches.name: Brute
approaches.idea: Nested loops: for each dept, for each job_title, count matching rows.

code.code:
SELECT d.dept_id, j.job_title,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id AND e.job_title = j.job_title) AS emp_count
FROM departments d
CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT job_title FROM employees) j
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id AND e.job_title = j.job_title)
ORDER BY d.dept_id, j.job_title;
code.mysql:
SELECT d.dept_id, j.job_title,
  (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id AND e.job_title = j.job_title) AS emp_count
FROM departments d
CROSS JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT job_title FROM employees) j
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.dept_id AND e.job_title = j.job_title)
ORDER BY d.dept_id, j.job_title;

approaches.cost: O(depts × jobs × employees) — catastrophic for real data. Only works because dataset is tiny.
approaches.pitfalls: CROSS JOIN explodes combinations. Correlated subquery re-scans for each pair.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Multi-column GROUP BY — single pass, hash on (dept_id, job_title) composite key.

code.code:
SELECT dept_id, job_title, COUNT(*) AS emp_count
FROM employees
GROUP BY dept_id, job_title
ORDER BY dept_id, job_title;
code.mysql: SELECT dept_id, job_title, COUNT(*) AS emp_count FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id, job_title ORDER BY dept_id, job_title;

approaches.cost: One scan + hash aggregate on composite key. O(n) time. Optimal for any data size.

exercise.solution: SELECT dept_id, job_title, COUNT(*) AS emp_count FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id, job_title ORDER BY dept_id, job_title;

blocks.title: GROUP BY dept_id with COUNT, SUM, AVG

stages.label: FROM employees
stages.sql: SELECT emp_id, dept_id, salary FROM employees;

stages.label: WHERE (none — all rows)
stages.sql: SELECT emp_id, dept_id, salary FROM employees;
stages.note: No WHERE clause, all 21 rows pass through

stages.label: GROUP BY dept_id
stages.sql: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt, SUM(salary) AS total, AVG(salary) AS avg FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id;
stages.note: Rows collapse into 6 groups (dept_id 1–6). Research (dept_id=7) has no employees → no group

stages.label: HAVING (none)
stages.sql: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt, SUM(salary) AS total, AVG(salary) AS avg FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id;
stages.note: No HAVING filter, all 6 groups retained

stages.label: SELECT + ORDER BY
stages.sql: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) AS cnt, SUM(salary) AS total, ROUND(AVG(salary)::numeric,2) AS avg FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id ORDER BY dept_id;
stages.note: Final projection with rounding; 6 rows returned ordered by dept_id

sections.title: Trap — COUNT(*) vs COUNT(col) with NULLs

blocks.claim: COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) always return the same number.
blocks.refutation: COUNT(*) counts all rows. COUNT(column) counts only non-NULL values in that column. When the column has NULLs, the results differ.
blocks.correctModel: Use COUNT(*) for row counts. Use COUNT(col) when you specifically need non-NULL count of that column.

evidence.label: proof on hr data
evidence.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS all_rows, COUNT(manager_id) AS non_null_mgrs FROM employees;
-- Returns: all_rows=21, non_null_mgrs=20 (Anita Rao CEO has NULL manager_id)

glossary.def: Computes single value from multiple rows: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX.
Collapses rows with same key values into one row per group.
